content:
Hand osteoarthritis commonly affects the joints at the end and middle of the fingers and the base of the thumb. It causes pain, stiffness, knobbly swellings and weaker grip, and is most common in women over 50. It cannot be cured, but hand exercises, anti-inflammatory gels, splints and gadgets help most people. Surgery is occasionally needed for the thumb.

Which joints are affected

  • the joints nearest the fingertips (DIP joints). Bony lumps here are called Heberden's nodes.
  • the middle finger joints (PIP joints). Lumps here are called Bouchard's nodes.
  • the base of the thumb (CMC joint). Causes pain when gripping, pinching, opening jars or turning keys.

The knuckles where the fingers meet the hand are less often affected by osteoarthritis. Swelling there is more typical of rheumatoid arthritis.

Symptoms

  • pain, especially when using your hands
  • stiffness, usually lasting less than 30 minutes in the morning
  • knobbly swellings that may be red and tender while they develop, then settle
  • reduced grip and pinch strength
  • fingers that bend to one side
  • difficulty with fine tasks such as buttons, writing or opening packets

Symptoms are often worst in the first few years and may become less painful over time, even if the lumps remain.

Diagnosis

NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms and examination without an X-ray. See your GP if you have swelling of the knuckles, a lot of morning stiffness, or symptoms in several joints on both hands, as these can suggest inflammatory arthritis.

Exercises

Regular hand exercises help keep fingers moving and maintain strength. Try these each day:

  • make a fist: gently curl your fingers into a loose fist, then stretch them out straight
  • thumb touches: touch the tip of your thumb to each fingertip in turn
  • finger spreads: place your hand flat on a table and spread your fingers apart
  • tabletop: bend your knuckles while keeping your fingers straight, then relax
  • putty or a soft ball: squeeze gently to build grip strength

Warm your hands in warm water first if they are stiff.

Pain relief

NICE recommends topical NSAID gels as a first option for hand osteoarthritis. Rub a small amount into the sore joints. Ask your pharmacist if they are suitable for you. Some people use painkillers for flares. Heat, such as a warm water soak or paraffin wax bath, can ease stiffness.

Splints and support

A thumb splint can ease pain at the base of the thumb by supporting it during activity or at night. An occupational therapist or hand therapist can advise and fit one. Ask your GP for a referral, or check whether you can self-refer.

Gadgets and joint protection

  • jar and bottle openers
  • thick-handled cutlery, pens and kitchen utensils
  • tap turners and key turners
  • lever-style door handles
  • electric can openers and lightweight kettles
  • spreading the load across both hands

Many of these are inexpensive and available from chemists and supermarkets.

Injections and surgery

Steroid injections may be offered for a very painful thumb base joint. Surgery is sometimes offered when thumb base arthritis remains severe despite other treatments. The most common operation removes a small bone at the base of the thumb. Finger joint surgery is less common.

Conditions that can look similar

  • carpal tunnel syndrome, causing tingling and numbness in the thumb and fingers
  • trigger finger, where a finger catches when bending
  • De Quervain's tenosynovitis, causing pain at the thumb side of the wrist
  • rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis

Living with hand osteoarthritis

Pace tasks that use your hands, take breaks and switch between activities. Keeping your hands moving every day helps more than resting them completely. Talk to your employer about adjustments if your work involves a lot of hand use.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
